name: Texas

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Texas became the 28th state on December 29, 1845. Congress gave it 2 seats in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, Texas kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 2 to 4 seats.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 4 to 6 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 43rd Congress (1873–1875), Texas elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 6 to 11 seats.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 11 to 13 seats.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 13 to 16 seats.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 16 to 18 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 63rd through 65th Congresses (1913–1919), Texas elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 18 to 21 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 73rd Congress (1933–1935), Texas elected 3 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Texas kept 21 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 21 to 22 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 83rd through 85th Congresses (1953–1959), Texas elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 22 to 23 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 88th through 89th Congresses (1963–1967), Texas elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 23 to 24 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: White v. Weiser
events.text: The Supreme Court struck down Texas's congressional map for population differences that could have been avoided.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 24 to 27 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 27 to 30 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Bush v. Vera
events.text: The Supreme Court held that Districts 18, 29 and 30 were racial gerrymanders. A lower court then redrew 13 districts and voided their March primaries; those seats were filled in special elections in November 1996 under the new lines.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 30 to 32 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Mid-decade redistricting
events.text: The legislature replaced the court-drawn 2002 map with a new one in October 2003, after a regular session and three special sessions, during two of which some legislators left the state to block a quorum. The map was used from the 2004 election.

events.title: LULAC v. Perry
events.text: The Supreme Court upheld most of the 2003 map but held that District 23 violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. A court redrew it and nearby districts for the 2006 election.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 32 to 36 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Abbott v. Perez
events.text: The Supreme Court reversed most of a lower court ruling against Texas's 2013 maps, finding the lower court had wrongly presumed the legislature acted with discriminatory intent.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Texas's House delegation grew from 36 to 38 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: LULAC v. Abbott
events.text: On November 18, 2025 a three-judge federal court in El Paso found the 2025 map was a racial gerrymander and blocked its use. On December 4, 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that ruling, and in April 2026 it reversed it.

events.title: Mid-decade redistricting
events.text: In August 2025 the legislature passed a new congressional map in a special session, and the governor signed it on August 29. It redrew districts in the Houston, Dallas–Fort Worth, Austin and South Texas areas, and after the Supreme Court stayed a lower-court ruling against it, it was used in the 2026 election.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c037.text: Texas sent no members to the 37th Congress (1861–1863), so the map shows only its outline and no districts.

c041.text: Texas's 1869 constitution set out a new map of four congressional districts. It was used when Texas members were seated again after the Civil War; none had been seated since 1861.

c043.text: After the 1870 census raised Texas's seats from 4 to 6, the state kept its existing districts and elected 2 members statewide (at-large).

c044.text: In 1874 the legislature drew six districts, moving into districts the two seats added by the 1870 apportionment, which had been filled statewide in 1872.

c047.text: In 1879 the legislature passed the 1874 six-district map again with clarified wording, and that version was used in the 1880 election.

c048.text: New map drawn after the 1880 census, which raised Texas's seats from 6 to 11. It was first used in the 1882 election.

c050.text: Texas's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1886 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c053.text: New map drawn after the 1890 census, which raised Texas's seats from 11 to 13. It was first used in the 1892 election.

c055.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in one district from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c058.text: New map drawn after the 1900 census, which raised Texas's seats from 13 to 16. It was first used in the 1902 election.

c062.text: In 1909 the legislature enacted a new 16-district plan, replacing the one it had passed in 1901, in time for the 1910 election.

c066.text: The two seats Texas gained in the 1910 census apportionment were elected statewide until the legislature enacted an 18-district plan in 1917. That plan stayed in use through 1932.

c073.text: After the 1930 census raised Texas's seats from 18 to 21, the state kept its existing districts and elected 3 members statewide (at-large).

c074.text: The three seats added in the 1930 apportionment were elected statewide in 1932. In 1933 the legislature enacted a 21-district plan (Senate Bill 195), used through the 1956 election.

c083.text: After the 1950 census raised Texas's seats from 21 to 22, the state kept its existing districts and elected one member statewide (at-large).

c086.text: The seat added in the 1950 apportionment was elected statewide until the legislature passed House Bill 229 in 1957, creating a 22-district plan first used in 1958.

c088.text: After the 1960 census raised Texas's seats from 22 to 23, the state kept its existing districts and elected one member statewide (at-large).

c090.text: In Bush v. Martin (1963) a federal court held Texas's congressional districts violated one person, one vote, and the Supreme Court affirmed. The legislature then passed a 23-district plan (House Bill 67) in 1965, which the court accepted.

c091.text: In 1967 the legislature enacted Senate Bill 335, a revised version of the 1965 plan, while the federal court in Bush v. Martin kept jurisdiction over later changes. It was used for the 1968 and 1970 elections.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which raised Texas's seats from 23 to 24. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c094.text: Following the Supreme Court's 1973 decision in White v. Weiser, a federal court ordered a new 24-district plan (Plan B), which was used for the 1974 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which raised Texas's seats from 24 to 27. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c099.text: The 1982 election used a map partly redrawn by a federal court in Seamon v. Upham after the Justice Department objected to two South Texas districts. In 1983 the legislature passed Senate Bill 480, a 27-district plan used from 1984 through 1990.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which raised Texas's seats from 27 to 30. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c105.text: New map following: Bush v. Vera. The Supreme Court held that Districts 18, 29 and 30 were racial gerrymanders. A lower court then redrew 13 districts and voided their March primaries; those seats were filled in special elections in November 1996 under the new lines.

c108.text: After the 2000 census raised Texas's seats from 30 to 32 and the legislature did not pass a congressional map, a federal court drew one in Balderas v. Texas (2001). It was used in the 2002 election.

c109.text: New map following: Mid-decade redistricting. The legislature replaced the court-drawn 2002 map with a new one in October 2003, after a regular session and three special sessions, during two of which some legislators left the state to block a quorum. The map was used from the 2004 election.

c110.text: New map following: LULAC v. Perry. The Supreme Court upheld most of the 2003 map but held that District 23 violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. A court redrew it and nearby districts for the 2006 election.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which raised Texas's seats from 32 to 36. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c115.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 9 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c118.text: New map drawn after the 2020 census, which raised Texas's seats from 36 to 38. It was first used in the 2022 election.

c120.text: New map following: Mid-decade redistricting. In August 2025 the legislature passed a new congressional map in a special session, and the governor signed it on August 29. It redrew districts in the Houston, Dallas–Fort Worth, Austin and South Texas areas, and after the Supreme Court stayed a lower-court ruling against it, it was used in the 2026 election.
